results.title: Modal formulas
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a type $\alpha$ of atoms, the formulas of basic modal logic over $\alpha$ are generated as follows: every atom $p \in \alpha$ is a formula; falsity $\bot$ is a formula; if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are formulas then so is the implication $\varphi \to \psi$; and if $\varphi$ is a formula then so is the necessity formula $\Box\varphi$.

results.title: Kripke model
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A Kripke model consists of a nonempty collection of worlds, an accessibility relation, and an atom valuation.

results.title: Satisfaction in a Kripke model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model with accessibility relation $R$. Satisfaction of a modal formula at a world $w$ of $M$ is defined by recursion on the formula: $w$ satisfies an atom $p$ if and only if the valuation of $M$ makes $p$ true at $w$; $w$ never satisfies $\bot$; $w$ satisfies $\varphi \to \psi$ if and only if $w$ satisfies $\psi$ whenever it satisfies $\varphi$; and $w$ satisfies $\Box\varphi$ if and only if…

results.title: Global validity in a Kripke model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A formula $\varphi$ is globally valid in a Kripke model $M$ when $\varphi$ is satisfied at every world of $M$.

results.title: Falsity is valid in no Kripke model
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Kripke model $M$, the formula $\bot$ is not valid in $M$: since $M$ has at least one world and no world satisfies $\bot$, some world of $M$ fails to satisfy $\bot$.

results.title: Semantics of possibility
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model with accessibility relation $R$, and let $\Diamond\varphi$ denote the formula $
eg\Box
eg\varphi$, where $
eg\chi$ is $\chi 	o  ot$. For every world $w$ and modal formula $\varphi$, $w$ satisfies $\Diamond\varphi$ in $M$ if and only if there is a world $v$ with $w \mathrel{R} v$ such that $v$ satisfies $\varphi$ in $M$.

results.title: Validity of axiom K on Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The K axiom is valid on every Kripke model.

results.title: Axiom T is valid on reflexive Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose accessibility relation $R$ is reflexive: $R\,w\,w$ for every world $w$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the T axiom $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$ is globally valid in $M$.

results.title: Axiom 4 is valid on transitive Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose accessibility relation $R$ is transitive: $R\,u\,v$ and $R\,v\,w$ imply $R\,u\,w$ for all worlds $u, v, w$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the 4 axiom $\Box\varphi \to \Box\Box\varphi$ is globally valid in $M$.

results.title: Axiom D is valid on serial Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose accessibility relation $R$ is serial: every world $w$ has some world $v$ with $R\,w\,v$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the D axiom $\Box\varphi \to \Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\varphi$ abbreviates $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, is globally valid in $M$.

results.title: Axiom B is valid on symmetric Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose accessibility relation $R$ is symmetric: $R\,u\,v$ implies $R\,v\,u$ for all worlds $u, v$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the B axiom $\varphi \to \Box\Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\varphi$ abbreviates $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, is globally valid in $M$.

results.title: Axiom 5 is valid on euclidean Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose accessibility relation $R$ is euclidean: $R\,u\,v$ and $R\,u\,w$ imply $R\,v\,w$ for all worlds $u, v, w$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the 5 axiom $\Diamond\varphi \to \Box\Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\varphi$ abbreviates $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, is globally valid in $M$.

results.title: Bounded morphism
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be Kripke models over the same atoms, with sets of worlds $W$ and $V$ and accessibility relations $R_M$ and $R_N$. A bounded morphism from $M$ to $N$ is a map $f : W \to V$ such that every atom holds at a world $w$ in $M$ if and only if it holds at $f(w)$ in $N$; whenever $w \mathrel{R_M} w'$, also $f(w) \mathrel{R_N} f(w')$ (forth); and whenever $f(w) \mathrel{R_N} v'$, there is a world $w'$ with…

results.title: Extensionality for bounded morphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Two bounded morphisms $f$ and $g$ between the same Kripke models are equal if $f(w) = g(w)$ for every world $w$.

results.title: Identity bounded morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every Kripke model $M$, the identity map on the worlds of $M$ is a bounded morphism from $M$ to itself.

results.title: Composition of bounded morphisms
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M_1$, $M_2$, $M_3$ be Kripke models over the same atoms. If $f$ is a bounded morphism from $M_1$ to $M_2$ and $g$ is a bounded morphism from $M_2$ to $M_3$, then the composite map $g \circ f$ on worlds is a bounded morphism from $M_1$ to $M_3$.

results.title: Invariance of modal satisfaction under bounded morphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a bounded morphism from a Kripke model $M$ to a Kripke model $N$ over the same atoms. Then for every modal formula $\varphi$ and every world $w$ of $M$, $w$ satisfies $\varphi$ in $M$ if and only if $f(w)$ satisfies $\varphi$ in $N$.

results.title: Surjective bounded morphisms preserve and reflect validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be Kripke models over the same atoms and let $f$ be a bounded morphism from $M$ to $N$ whose map on worlds is surjective. Then for every formula $\varphi$, $\varphi$ is globally valid in $M$ if and only if $\varphi$ is globally valid in $N$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 14.102(a): non-injective braid endomorphisms with non-cyclic image
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for some $n > 4$ the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands has a non-injective endomorphism whose image is not cyclic (in particular not trivial). Posed by V. Lin and V. Shpilrain.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 14.102(b): endomorphisms of the braid commutator subgroup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every $n > 4$, every endomorphism of the commutator subgroup $[B_n, B_n]$ of the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands other than the trivial endomorphism is bijective, that is, an automorphism. Posed by V. Lin and V. Shpilrain.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 14.102(c): torsion-free quotients of braid groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every $n > 4$, the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands has a nontrivial normal subgroup $N$ such that the quotient $B_n / N$ is non-abelian and torsion-free (no element other than the identity has finite order). Posed by V. Lin and V. Shpilrain.

results.title: Non-injective endomorphisms of braid groups on five or more strands have cyclic image
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The answer to Kourovka Problem 14.102(a) is negative: there is no $n > 4$ for which the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands has a non-injective endomorphism whose image is not cyclic. Equivalently, for every $n \ge 5$, every non-injective endomorphism of $B_n$ has cyclic image.

results.title: Degree-normalized absolute value at a finite place

results.title: Degree-normalized absolute value at an infinite place

results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $d = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ and let $v$ be an infinite place of $K$, with absolute value $|\cdot|_v$ and multiplicity $m_v$, equal to $1$ if $v$ is real and $2$ if $v$ is complex. results.title: Value of the degree-normalized absolute value at an infinite place
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $d = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ and let $v$ be an infinite place of $K$, with absolute value $|\cdot|_v$ and multiplicity $m_v$, equal to $1$ if $v$ is real and $2$ if $v$ is complex. For every $x \in K$, the degree-normalized absolute value of $x$ at $v$ equals $|x|_v^{m_v/d}$.

results.title: Degree-normalized absolute value at a real place
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $d = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ and let $v$ be a real infinite place of $K$, with absolute value $|\cdot|_v$. For every $x \in K$, the degree-normalized absolute value of $x$ at $v$ equals $|x|_v^{1/d}$.

results.title: Degree-normalized absolute value at a complex place

results.title: Places of a number field
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a number field $K$, the places of $K$ form the disjoint union of the infinite places of $K$ (the absolute values coming from complex embeddings of $K$) and the finite places of $K$ (the absolute values coming from nonzero prime ideals of the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$).

results.title: Infinite places as places
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a number field $K$, each infinite place $v$ of $K$ is regarded as a place of $K$ via the inclusion of the infinite places into the disjoint union of the infinite and finite places of $K$.

results.title: Finite places as places
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a number field $K$, each finite place $v$ of $K$ is regarded as a place of $K$ via the inclusion of the finite places into the disjoint union of the infinite and finite places of $K$.

results.title: Residue norm of a finite place
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $v$ be a finite place of a number field $K$ and $\mathfrak{p}_v$ the corresponding nonzero prime ideal of the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. The residue norm $N(v)$ is the absolute norm $|\mathcal{O}_K / \mathfrak{p}_v|$ of $\mathfrak{p}_v$, the cardinality of the residue field at $v$, regarded as a real number.

results.title: The Collatz map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Collatz map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ sends a natural number $n$ to $n / 2$ if $n$ is even and to $3n + 1$ if $n$ is odd.

results.title: Iterates of the Collatz map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the Collatz map, which sends $n$ to $n / 2$ if $n$ is even and to $3n + 1$ if $n$ is odd. For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the $k$-th Collatz iterate of $n$ is $T^k(n)$, the result of applying $T$ to $n$ exactly $k$ times: $T^0(n) = n$ and $T^{k+1}(n) = T(T^k(n))$.

results.title: Collatz stopping time
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the Collatz map, which sends $n$ to $n / 2$ if $n$ is even and to $3n + 1$ if $n$ is odd, and let $T^k$ denote its $k$-fold iterate, with $T^0(n) = n$. For a natural number $n$, the Collatz stopping time of $n$ is undefined if $n = 0$ or if $T^k(n) \ne 1$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$; otherwise it is the least $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $T^k(n) = 1$.

results.title: Division by $q$ in $\mathbb{F}_2((q))$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a power series $x = \sum_n x_n q^n \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, its shift is the power series $\sum_n x_{n+1} q^n$, obtained by discarding the constant term of $x$ and dividing by $q$. In particular, the shift of $qy$ is $y$ for every $y \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$.

results.title: Dividing a multiple of $q$ by $q$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every power series $y \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, applying the shift $\sum_n x_n q^n \mapsto \sum_n x_{n+1} q^n$ to $qy$ gives back $y$.

results.title: The q-analog of the 3x+1 map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a power series $y = \sum_n y_n q^n \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, write $y/q$ for the power series $\sum_n y_{n+1} q^n$: the constant term of $y$ is discarded and the rest is divided by $q$. For power series $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the map $T_{A,B} : \mathbb{F}_2[[q]] \to \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ is defined by $T_{A,B}(x) = x/q$ if the constant term of $x$ is $0$, and $T_{A,B}(x) = (Ax + B)/q$ otherwise.

results.title: The q-analog 3x+1 map on multiples of $q$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all power series $A, B, y \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the $q$-analog $3x+1$ map satisfies $T_{A,B}(qy) = y$.

results.title: $3x + 1$ is even for odd $2$-adic $x$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $2$-adic integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ whose residue modulo $2$ is nonzero, the residue of $3x + 1$ modulo $2$ is zero.

results.title: The $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The map $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ is defined by $T(x) = x/2$ if $x$ is even and $T(x) = (3x+1)/2$ if $x$ is odd, where even and odd refer to the residue of $x$ modulo $2$.

results.title: Even branch of the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ be the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers. For every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ whose residue modulo $2$ is zero, $2\,T(x) = x$.

results.title: Odd branch of the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ be the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers. For every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ whose residue modulo $2$ is nonzero, $2\,T(x) = 3x + 1$.

results.title: The $2$-adic $3x+1$ map swaps $1$ and $2$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The $2$-adic $3x+1$ map $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ satisfies $T(1) = 2$ and $T(2) = 1$.

results.title: The parity vector of the q-analog 3x+1 map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For power series $A, B, x \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the parity vector of $x$ is the $2$-adic integer $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} x_k 2^k \in \mathbb{Z}_2$, where $x_k \in \{0, 1\}$ is the constant coefficient of the $k$-th iterate $T_{A,B}^k(x)$ of the $q$-analog $3x+1$ map $T_{A,B}$.

results.title: The parity vector of $0$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the parity vector of $0$ under the $q$-analog $T_{A,B}$ of the $3x+1$ map is $0$, that is, $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(0) = 0$.

results.title: The $q$-Collatz map is conjugate to the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be odd power series in $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ (constant term $1$), let $T_{A,B}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map on $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, and let $T$ be the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_2$. Then there is a bijection $h : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $h^{-1}(T_{A,B}(h(x))) = T(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$.

results.summary: Let $T_q = T_{1+q,1}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map with $A = 1 + q$ and $B = 1$, so that $T_q(x) = x/q$ if $q$ divides $x$ and $T_q(x) = ((1+q)x + 1)/q$ otherwise, and let $T$ be the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_2$. Then there is a bijection $h : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $h^{-1}(T_q(h(x))) = T(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$.

results.title: Polynomial orbits of $T_{1,1+q^2}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T = T_{1,1+q^2}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map with $A = 1$ and $B = 1 + q^2$. For every polynomial $p$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, some iterate $T^k(p)$ with $k \ge 0$ lies in $\{0, 1 + q, 1, q\}$, the set formed by the fixed points $0$ and $1 + q$ of $T$ and its $2$-cycle $\{1, q\}$. Moreover, for every $x \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, $T(x)$ is a polynomial if and only if $x$ is a polynomial.

results.title: A perturbation at $q^{n+1}$ moves to $q^n$ under $T_{A,B}$

Then there is an odd power series $W \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $T_{A,B}(U + q^{n+1} V) = T_{A,B}(U) + q^n W$.

results.summary: Let $A, B, U, V$ be power series in $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $A$, $B$ and $V$ odd (constant term $1$), let $T_{A,B}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $k \le n + 1$. results.title: Parity vectors detect congruence modulo $q^{n+1}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ be odd (constant term $1$), let $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}$ be the parity vector map of the $q$-analog $T_{A,B}$ of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n \ge 0$ be an integer. For all $a, b \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, we have $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(a) \equiv \mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(b) \pmod{2^{n+1}}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ if and only if $q^{n+1}$ divides $a - b$.

results.title: Parity vectors induce bijections modulo $q^n$
results.caption: Theorem

Then there is a bijection $e : \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]/(q^n) \to \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ such that, for every $a \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, $e$ sends the class of $a$ to the residue of $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(a)$ modulo $2^n$.

results.title: Fixed points and the $2$-cycle of the $q$-Collatz map

results.title: Center of a vertex set under a coloring
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a proper vertex coloring of a simple graph $G$, let $s$ be a set of vertices of $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex of $G$. Then $v$ is a $\varphi$-center of $s$ if $v \in s$ and no other vertex of $s$ has the color $\varphi(v)$.

results.title: Centered coloring
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A proper vertex coloring $\varphi$ of a simple graph $G$ is centered if, for every set $s$ of vertices of $G$ whose induced subgraph is connected, some vertex is a $\varphi$-center of $s$.

results.title: Centers via unique existence

results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a proper vertex coloring of a simple graph $G$, let $s$ be a set of vertices of $G$ and let $v$ be a vertex of $G$. Then $v$ is a $\varphi$-center of $s$ if and only if $v \in s$ and there is exactly one vertex $u \in s$ with $\varphi(u) = \varphi(v)$.

results.title: Cached height of an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The cached height of the empty tree is $0$, and the cached height of a node is the height value stored at that node, so it is read off the root in constant time.

results.title: AVL node with computed height
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Given trees $L$ and $R$ and a key $k$, this is the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$.

results.title: Correct cached heights
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty tree has correct cached heights. A node storing the height $c$, with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$, has correct cached heights when $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights and $c = \max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree).

results.title: AVL balance invariant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty tree is balanced. A node with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$ is balanced when $\ell$ and $r$ are balanced and $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree). Equivalently, at every node the balance factor $h(\ell) - h(r)$ lies in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type. Erasing the cached heights sends a tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ to a binary tree over $\alpha$: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with height $h$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are the erasures of $L$ and $R$.

results.title: Membership in an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A key $x$ belongs to a tree $T$ when $x$ belongs to the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights. Equivalently, no key belongs to the empty tree, and $x$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $x$ belongs to $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ belongs to $R$.

results.title: Every key of an AVL tree satisfies a predicate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds when $p$ holds at the key of every node of $t$. It is defined as the corresponding predicate on the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights.

results.title: Ordered AVL trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached heights is an ordered binary search tree: the empty tree is ordered, and a node with key $k$ is ordered when its left and right subtrees are ordered, every key of the left subtree is less than $k$, and every key of the right subtree is greater than $k$.

results.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree onto a suffix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the list of keys of $t$ in inorder (left subtree, root key, right subtree, recursively) followed by $s$. It is computed in linear time by the binary search tree traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased.

results.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The inorder traversal of a tree $t$ lists its keys with the left subtree first, then the root key, then the right subtree, recursively. It is the binary search tree inorder traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased, computed in linear time.

results.title: AVL membership is membership in the underlying binary tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A key $x$ lies in a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights.

results.title: The all-keys predicate is unchanged by erasing height caches
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p$ holds at every key of the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights. This holds by definition.

results.title: Order of an AVL tree via its underlying binary tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing the cached heights is an ordered binary search tree.

results.title: AVL inorder traversal agrees with the erased binary search tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every AVL tree $t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary search tree inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights; this holds by definition.

results.title: Membership search in an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and a key $x$, the search for $x$ returns false on the empty tree; at a node with key $k$ it searches the left subtree if $x < k$, searches the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise. The cached heights are ignored.

results.title: AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For trees $l$, $r$ with cached heights and a key $x$, write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree) and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node with left subtree $A$, key $y$, right subtree $B$ and cached height $\max(h(A), h(B)) + 1$. The node $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is defined by cases. If $h(l) > h(r) + 1$ and $l$ has left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, it is the…

results.title: Insertion into an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives the node with key $x$, two empty children and cached height $1$. Inserting $x$ into a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ gives $\mathrm{balance}(L', k, R)$, where $L'$ is the result of…

results.title: Building an AVL tree from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the tree built from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ is obtained by AVL insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$. Thus the list is inserted from right to left, starting from the empty tree.

results.title: The all-keys predicate in terms of membership (AVL trees)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x \in t$, where $x \in t$ means that $x$ is the key of some node of $t$.

results.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of an AVL tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A key $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in $T$.

results.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree is strictly increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered, then in the inorder traversal of $t$ every key is less than every key that comes after it.

results.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree has no duplicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if an AVL tree is ordered, then its inorder traversal contains no key twice.

results.title: The AVL node constructor preserves cached heights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$ where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root (and $0$ for the empty tree), also has correct cached heights.

results.title: The AVL node constructor preserves balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\ell$ and $r$ be AVL trees that satisfy the AVL balance invariant, and write $h(\ell)$ and $h(r)$ for the heights cached at their roots (with height $0$ for the empty tree). If $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, satisfies the AVL balance invariant.

results.title: Rebalancing when the heights of the children differ by at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 1$, then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is the node with left subtree $l$, key $x$, right subtree $r$ and cached height $\max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$; no rotation is performed.

results.title: Single right rotation in AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $R$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(R) + 1 < c$ and…

results.title: Left-right double rotation in AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $R$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(R) + 1 < c$…

results.title: Single left rotation in AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(L) + 1 < c$ and…

results.title: Right-left double rotation in AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$, $C$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(L) + 1 < c$…

results.title: AVL rebalancing preserves cached heights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the tree produced by the rebalancing function from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ also has correct cached heights.

results.title: Upper bound on height after AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, and write $h$ for the cached height. Then for every key $k$, the rebalanced node $b$ built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ satisfies $h(b) \le \max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$.

results.title: Rebalancing does not drop below the taller child
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. If $L$ and $R$ are trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, then for every key $k$ we have $\max(h(L), h(R)) \le h(\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R))$.

results.title: AVL rebalancing yields a balanced tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are correct at every node and which are balanced (at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one), let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 2$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 2$, then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is balanced.

results.title: AVL rebalancing preserves the inorder traversal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, the inorder traversal of the rebalanced node built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ is the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.

results.title: Membership after AVL rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. For trees $L$ and $R$ and keys $k$ and $x$, the key $x$ lies in $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ if and only if $x$ lies in $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ lies in $R$.

results.title: Rebalancing an AVL node preserves the search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $k \in \alpha$, and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered trees with cached heights over $\alpha$ such that every key of $L$ is less than $k$ and every key of $R$ is greater than $k$. Then the tree that rebalancing produces from left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ is ordered.

results.title: AVL insertion preserves cached heights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If an AVL tree $t$ over $\alpha$ has correct cached heights, then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also has correct cached heights.

results.title: Upper bound on height after AVL insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if a tree $t$ has correct cached heights at every node, then for every key $x$ the cached height of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$ plus one.

results.title: Insertion does not lower the height
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Let the keys be linearly ordered, and let $T$ be a tree whose cached heights are correct at every node and which satisfies the AVL balance invariant at every node. Then for every key $x$, if $T'$ is the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$, we have $h(T) \le h(T')$.

results.title: AVL insertion preserves balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be an AVL tree over $\alpha$ and let $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ has correct cached heights and satisfies the AVL balance invariant, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also satisfies the AVL balance invariant.

results.title: Membership after insertion into an AVL tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key $y$ lies in the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into a tree $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ lies in $T$.

results.title: AVL insertion preserves the search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every key $x \in \alpha$ and every ordered tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.

results.title: Correctness of AVL search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered AVL tree over $\alpha$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, searching for $x$ in $t$ by following comparisons from the root returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.

results.title: AVL trees built from a list have correct cached heights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion has correct cached heights.

results.title: AVL trees built from a list are balanced
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion satisfies the AVL balance invariant.

results.title: AVL trees built from a list are ordered
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $xs$ one at a time, from the last element to the first, is ordered.

results.title: Membership in an AVL tree built from a list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key lies in the tree obtained by inserting the entries of a list one at a time, from last to first, into the empty tree exactly when it is in the list.

results.title: Leftmost key of a tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a default value $d$ and a binary tree $T$ with cached heights, the leftmost key of $T$ with default $d$ is $d$ when $T$ is empty; when $T$ has left subtree $L$ and root key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $L$ with default $k$. Thus for a nonempty tree it is the key of the node reached from the root by following left children as far as possible, and it does not depend on $d$.

results.title: Removing the leftmost key of an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree $t$ with cached heights, the tree obtained by removing the leftmost key of $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree stays empty. A node whose left subtree is empty is replaced by its right subtree. A node with nonempty left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ is replaced by $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where $l'$ is $l$ with its leftmost key removed and $\mathrm{balance}$ is the AVL…

results.title: Minimum deletion in an AVL tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Minimum deletion maps a binary tree with cached heights to the tree obtained by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up. It is the operation of removing the minimum, under the name used for the successor step of deletion, where a deleted node with two children is replaced by the minimum of its right subtree.

results.title: AVL tree deletion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. Deleting $x$ from a tree with cached heights is defined by recursion on the tree, where $\mathrm{balance}$ denotes the AVL rebalancing function. The empty tree stays empty. For a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where $l'$ is $l$ with $x$ deleted; if $k < x$, the result is…

results.title: AVL tree deletion under its alternative name
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$ is defined to be $\mathrm{erase}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$.

results.title: The leftmost key lies in the tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every nonempty binary tree $T$ with cached heights and every default value $d$, the leftmost key of $T$ computed with default $d$ occurs in $T$.

results.title: Removing the minimum keeps cached heights correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, are again correct.

results.title: Removing the leftmost key does not increase the height of an AVL tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $t$ is a tree whose cached heights are correct, then the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key is at most the cached height of $t$.

results.title: Removing the leftmost key lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $t$ is a tree whose cached heights are correct and which is balanced, then the cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.

results.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, is again balanced.

results.title: Removing the leftmost key preserves search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree obtained from $T$ by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up.

results.title: Keys left after removing the minimum exceed it
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, and suppose $t$ is ordered: at every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger than the key at that node. Let $m$ be the leftmost key of $t$, or an arbitrary default value if $t$ is empty. Then every key of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its…

results.title: The inorder traversal begins with the leftmost key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a nonempty tree with cached heights and $m$ its leftmost key. Then the inorder traversal of $t$ is $m$ followed by the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.

results.title: Deletion keeps cached heights correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.

results.title: Deletion does not increase the height of an AVL tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$.

results.title: Deletion lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a balanced tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.

results.title: Deletion preserves AVL balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.

results.title: AVL deletion preserves search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.

results.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.

results.title: AVL deletion keeps every other key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights whose keys come from a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs in $T$, then $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$. No search-tree ordering of $T$ is assumed.

results.title: Deletion removes the deleted key from an ordered AVL tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree. Then for every key $x$, $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$.

results.title: Keys of an ordered AVL tree after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ if and only if $y$ occurs in $T$ and $y \ne x$.

results.title: Deleting a key keeps cached heights correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.

results.title: Deleting a key preserves AVL balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.

results.title: Deleting a key from an ordered AVL tree keeps it ordered
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.

results.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion, alternative name
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$ under its alternative name, is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.

results.title: Minimum deletion keeps cached heights correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) are again correct.

results.title: Minimum deletion preserves AVL balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) is again balanced.

results.title: Successor-step minimum removal preserves search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree obtained by the minimum-removal step used for the successor in deletion, which removes the leftmost key of $T$ and rebalances on the way back up.
